title: Diagonal resilience of a sign matrix
text:
Recently, there have been major advances in random matrix theory, including Hu–Song–Wu’s sharp singularity asymptotic for random sign matrices and Xie’s proof of the Kahn–Komlós–Szemerédi conjecture on the linear dependence of fewer than n random sign vectors in ℝ^(n). Using results from these two papers, we can obtain a relatively simple proof of Vu’s diagonal resilience conjecture. In fact, the proof gives the following quantitative bound.

Reveal the off-diagonal entries of an n × n matrix, each an independent fair sign. Can you choose the diagonal signs to make it singular? Let P_(n) be the probability that at least one of the 2^(n) choices achieves this. For every fixed a > 0,

P_(n) = O(n^(−a)).

Van Vu first posed this question in 2006 alongside the more well-known conjecture on how many signs one must flip anywhere in the matrix to achieve singularity. Although the matching lower bound is still open, about n/2 flips typically suffice to copy one row onto another. The diagonal offers roughly twice that many flips, but only one per row and column. We will see this affects the problem greatly.

Two recent results

Let M have independent fair sign entries. Expose n − 1 columns and let H be their span over ℝ. Call a vertex of Q = {−1, 1}^(n) in H extra if it is different from the exposed columns and their negatives.

Xie. For every fixed b > 0, the probability that H contains any extra vertex is O(n^(−b)). (Theorem 3 and Remark 4.)

Hu–Song–Wu. A unit vector is compressible if it lies within distance ν of a vector supported on at most δn coordinates, for suitable fixed δ, ν > 0. Otherwise it is incompressible. Choose a unit normal Y to H using only the exposed columns. For constants L, η > 0 and all sufficiently large n,

$$\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb{P}\bigl(Y\text{ is incompressible and }|Y^\perp\cap Q|>L(n+1)^2\bigr)
     &\le 4^{-n},\\
 \mathbb{P}\bigl(M\text{ has a compressible left null vector}\bigr)
     &\le n(n-1)2^{-n}+2^{-n}e^{-\eta n}.
\end{aligned}$$

For the first bound, set q = D = 2 and h = 0 just before (5.6) and use the fact that, given the exposed columns, a fresh sign vector lands in Y^(⊥) with probability 2^(−n)|Y^(⊥) ∩ Q|. The second is Lemma 5.1 at t = 0 applied to M^(⊤). (Section 5.)

Counting singular diagonals

Let N count singular diagonal choices. A fresh random diagonal works with conditional probability N/2^(n), so Hu–Song–Wu’s Corollary 1.2 yields 𝔼N = 2^(n)ℙ(M is singular) ∼ 2n². How can there typically be none?

With probability 2^(−(n − 2)), the first two rows already agree in columns 3, 4, …, n. Should this happen, two diagonal signs are forced, and exactly 2^(n − 2) diagonals make the rows equal. This single relation contributes one in expectation.

For any pair of rows or columns, proportionality with a prescribed sign imposes n − 2 such constraints. A union bound over pairs and signs gives an upper bound of $4\binom{n}{2}2^{-(n-2)}$ for the probability that some diagonal produces a proportional pair. Let B be the event that M is singular with no proportional row or column pair. Fix a > 0. The expected number of diagonals giving B is 2^(n)ℙ(B), so it suffices to show

ℙ(B) = O(2^(−n)n^(−a)).   (1)

Leaving one column out

Expose every column except C_(j). Let V_(j) be the extra vertices in their span, and choose a unit normal Y_(j) to that span using only the exposed columns. On B there is a linear relation among the columns. Solving for any column with a nonzero coefficient puts it in the span of the others. Since no two are proportional, C_(j) ∈ V_(j) for at least one j.

Conditional on the exposure, C_(j) hits V_(j) with probability |V_(j)|/2^(n). Since V_(j) ⊆ Y_(j)^(⊥), an incompressible Y_(j) leaves at most L(n + 1)² targets outside an event of probability at most 4^(−n). We already know whether there are any targets when we draw C_(j). Taking expectations gives

ℙ(C_(j) ∈ V_(j), Y_(j) incompressible) ≤ 4^(−n) + L(n + 1)² 2^(−n)ℙ(V_(j) ≠ ⌀).

We use Xie’s result to bound the last probability by O(n^(−b)). Summing over j costs a factor of n, so b = a + 3 gives the required bound.

If C_(j) ∈ V_(j), then Y_(j) annihilates every column. A compressible Y_(j) therefore gives a compressible left null vector. Write K for the event that one exists, and R for the event of proportional rows. Each relation R_(i) = σR_(k), with σ = ±1, gives a two-coordinate left null vector $(e_i-\sigma e_k)/\sqrt{2}$, so R ⊆ K for large n. The n(n − 1) signed relations each have probability 2^(−n), and any two distinct ones intersect with probability at most 4^(−n). Hence ℙ(R) ≥ n(n − 1)2^(−n) − O(n⁴4^(−n)) by inclusion–exclusion. Subtracting this lower bound from the upper bound on ℙ(K) gives

ℙ(K \ R) ≤ 2^(−n)e^(−ηn) + O(n⁴4^(−n)).

Together the two cases prove (1). The chance of any diagonal giving B is at most 2^(n)ℙ(B) = O(n^(−a)). Adding the proportional-pair bound proves the theorem.

title: How many eigenvalues of a random sign matrix are real?
text:
I am very excited to announce that I have just uploaded my preprint, The Number of Real Eigenvalues of a Random Sign Matrix, to the arXiv. In it, I show that a typical large \(n\times n\) sign matrix has about \(\sqrt{2n/\pi}\) real eigenvalues.

Jean Ginibre studied a similar Gaussian model in 1965, where the entries are independent standard normal variables. In 1992, Edelman, Kostlan, and Shub showed that the expected number of real eigenvalues in the Gaussian model is asymptotic to \(\sqrt{2n/\pi}\). Their experiments with random sign matrices suggested the same leading term.

Terence Tao and Van Vu showed that the Gaussian prediction also holds for a wider class of matrices. For even \(n\), their theorem applies when the entries are independent, real, have sufficiently light tails, and match the first four moments of a standard normal.

In the discrete sign model, each entry is chosen independently and equally likely. Unfortunately, a fair sign matches the first three Gaussian moments, but the fourth power is \(1\), whereas a standard normal has a fourth moment of \(3\). Even this slight mismatch puts the simple sign model outside Tao and Vu’s theorem.

Vu conjectured that a typical sign matrix has on the order of \(\sqrt{n}\) real eigenvalues, likely asymptotically matching the Gaussian model. This can be intuited by thinking of discreteness at high numbers as simulating continuity, and yielding similar properties - such as the semicircle law. In 2025, Yi Han proved a lower bound with the same leading constant as the Gaussian.

My work gives the matching upper bound. If \(R_n\) counts the real eigenvalues, then

\[\frac{R_n}{\sqrt n}\longrightarrow\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\qquad\text{in }L^1.\]

This proves Vu’s conjecture and identifies the leading constant \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\).

Feel free to contact me with any questions or comments! For more on the four-moment theorem, I highly recommend Tao’s post about his work with Vu.

title: Finding a stable roommate
text:
Suppose that \(n\) people need roommates, with \(n\) even. Each person ranks the others in order of preference. We call a pairing stable if no two people in different rooms would rather ditch their roommates and pair off together. I have just uploaded to the arXiv a recent preprint in which Ian Studebaker and I study the probability \(P_n\) that a stable pairing exists when the rankings are independent and uniformly random.

This problem traces its beginnings to the famous stable marriage problem, where—as is common knowledge now—a stable pairing always exists. This problem can be thought of as a generalization of that, where there is no restriction on the sex of the person one is allowed to marry (as of 2015 in the U.S.). For this reason, I have also seen it referred to as the homosexual stable marriage problem. Initial interest in this problem was concentrated around algorithmic solutions, and Knuth even raised the possibility that deciding whether a stable pairing exists might be NP-complete! In 1985, Irving gave an \(O(n^2)\) algorithm that finds a stable pairing or determines that none exists.

Let us turn our attention to the probabilistic side of this problem. Boris Pittel showed in 1993 that the expected number of stable pairings tends to \(\sqrt{e}\). A single set of rankings can admit several stable pairings, so this average still leaves open how often a solution exists. Pittel also obtained the lower bound \(P_n \geq (2e^{3/2}+o(1))/\sqrt{\pi n}\).

Gusfield and Irving had conjectured that \(P_n\) tends to zero, and Stephan Mertens later conjectured that it decays on the order of \(n^{-1/4}\). Very recently, in January 2026, Byron Chin and Marcus Michelen resolved the first of these conjectures by proving that \(P_n \leq n^{-1/17}\) for all sufficiently large even \(n\).

We determine the rate of decay, along with the sharp constant. As \(n\) grows through even integers,

\[
P_n \sim \frac{e\,2^{1/4}\Gamma(3/4)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\,n^{-1/4}.
\]

Mertens gives an exact formula for \(p_\pi\), the probability that a given permutation \(\pi\) is stable. Summing \(p_\pi\) over permutations made up entirely of two-cycles gives the expected number of stable pairings. A single set of rankings can contribute several pairings to this sum. To correct for this overcount, Mertens gives an exact formula for \(P_n\) as an alternating sum of \(p_\pi\) over permutations whose cycles all have even length. Each cycle longer than two contributes a minus sign, and the positive and negative terms nearly cancel.

We group permutations by the number \(2k\) of people in longer cycles. After averaging over the rankings, symmetry makes the first-order correction to the stability probability dependent only on \(k\). This allows us to combine the signed contributions before estimating the remaining error. The leading term then reduces to a sum of positive terms, whose coefficients decay on the order of \(k^{-3/2}\), and a factor suppresses terms with \(k\) well below \(\sqrt{n}\). The tail on this scale has order \(n^{-1/4}\). Evaluating the limiting integral gives the constant.

title: How often is a random sign matrix normal?
text:
Suppose we fill an \(n \times n\) matrix with independent, uniformly random signs. What’s the probability that the resulting matrix is normal?
One way this can happen is for the matrix to be symmetric. Once we’ve chosen the entries above the diagonal, each entry below it has a one-half chance of matching its partner. So
\[
\Pr(M = M^\top) = 2^{-\binom{n}{2}}.
\]
How much do the nonsymmetric normal matrices add?
